Strangely said. The scholiast explains it somehow as συγγενεῖς, ἢ δειλαὶ, ὑπὸ μητέρων ἁπαλῶς τεθραμμέναι [kindred, or cowardly, delicately reared by mothers], which Weilius rightly judged could not have been said thus; to him one verse seems to have fallen out after these words. To me it seems more probable that τεθραμμέναι [reared] was introduced either from a gloss or to fill a lacuna in place of another word, such as ἀπ᾿ εὐγενῶν [from noble stock], or φυταλμίων [of the race], which Aeschylus used in Agam. 327 ἀνδρῶν κασιγνήτων τε καὶ φυταλμίων παῖδες γερόντων [children of men, brothers and of the race, of old men]. Why mothers alone are named, not fathers, can be understood from what Keil collected in Philologus vol. 16 p. 9.
For whom all the Asian land, having nourished them, groans with fierce longing.
Except the nature of the earth nourished by the Sun.
She reared a lion's whelp in the house, unweaned.
For a kindly host nourishes him.

For what has no mind, like a beast, must be nourished.
